item.description: 🏔 #OTD in 1814, Mikhail Lermontov – one of Russia’s greatest poets – was born in Moscow. His poetry spoke of love and loneliness, freedom and devotion to his Motherland with an intensity that continues to resonate with modern readers. 212 years after his birth, he remains one of the best-loved figures in Russian literature. Lermontov was born into a noble family and lost his mother in early childhood. Raised by his grandmother, Elizaveta Arsenyeva , at the Tarkhany estate (in what is now the village of Lermontovo in the Penza Region), he received a broad education at home before attending Moscow University’s boarding school for noble boys and then the University itself. By the age of 14, he was already writing poetry. The young poet also developed a lifelong passion for painting. From his childhood in the Penza Region to his visits to the Caucasus for treatment at the mineral springs of what is now Pyatigorsk , he found inspiration in the world around him. 🏔
#OTD
in 1814,
Mikhail Lermontov
– one of Russia’s greatest poets – was born in Moscow.
His poetry spoke of love and loneliness, freedom and devotion to his Motherland with an intensity that continues to resonate with modern readers.
212 years after his birth, he remains one of the best-loved figures in Russian literature.
Lermontov was born into a noble family
and lost his mother in early childhood. Raised by his grandmother,
Elizaveta Arsenyeva
, at
the Tarkhany estate
(in what is now the village of Lermontovo in the Penza Region), he received a broad education at home before attending
Moscow University’s boarding school for noble boys
and then
the University
itself.
By the age of 14, he was already writing poetry.
The young poet also developed a lifelong passion for painting.
From his childhood in
the Penza Region
to his visits to the Caucasus for treatment at the mineral springs of what is now
Pyatigorsk
, he found inspiration in the world around him. Working with pencil, watercolour and oils, he captured
landscapes, portraits and scenes of everyday life
. At times, impressions he first put on canvas resurfaced years later in his poetry.
✍️
During his lifetime, Lermontov wrote around 400 poems and 30 narrative poems, as well as plays and prose
. Among his most famous works are
Borodino
,
The Sail
,
The Demon
and
The Novice (Mtsyri)
, the four-act play
Masquerade
and his most celebrated novel
A Hero of Our Time
.
In 1837
, the death of Russia's greatest poet
Alexander Pushkin
in a duel prompted Lermontov to write
Death of the Poet
. Both a tribute to Pushkin and an indictment of the society he blamed for his death, the poem was copied by hand and passed from reader to reader.
It brought Lermontov widespread recognition – and the anger of the imperial court.
He was arrested and sent to serve in the Caucasus.
Proud, sensitive and sharp-witted
, Lermontov could be unsparing in his criticism of society and showed considerable courage as an army officer.
His attachment to the Caucasus began with childhood visits and lasted throughout his life
. Its mountains, people and legends inspired some of his finest writing.
🕯
On July 27, 1841, a fatal duel near Pyatigorsk cut his life short at just 26
. Yet even at that young age, Lermontov had created works that would secure
his place in the pantheon of Russian literature
.
Lermontov's figure stands on
the Millennium of Russia monument
(unveiled in 1862),
towns, streets and theatres bear his name
. Monuments honour him in Russia and abroad; even
a crater on Mercury
and
an asteroid
are named after him.
📖
His most enduring memorial, however, is
his writing
– still read, recited and loved by generations.
#DiscoverRUSSIA

item.title: 🇷🇺 On October 15, Foreign Minister of Russia Sergey Lavrov and Foreign Minister of Turkiye Hakan Fidan
item.description: 🇷🇺 🇹🇷 On October 15, Foreign Minister of Russia Sergey Lavrov and Foreign Minister of Turkiye Hakan Fidan held a meeting on the sidelines of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia ( #CICA ) Summit in Baku . The Ministers exchanged views on current priorities for strengthening trade, economic and energy cooperation , with a focus on progress in implementing key bilateral projects. They reaffirmed the importance of coordination between Russia and Turkiye on the international stage , including efforts to promote a just settlement of the crisis surrounding Ukraine. The Ministers also reviewed the schedule of upcoming contacts at the highest and other senior levels. #RussiaTurkiye

🎙
Statement
by Russian MFA Ambassador-at-Large
Rodion Miroshnik
during the dialogue with UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk at a plenary meeting of
the Third Committee of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly
(
New York, October 14, 2026
)
Read in full
Broadcast of the entire meeting
💬
We expect
an impartial and well-grounded assessment of events
from the High Commissioner for Human Rights, but we are not getting one.
The methodology used by OHCHR to collect and verify data, particularly on Ukraine,
raises very serious questions
.
In practice, OHCHR leaves data verification to third parties.
Questionable conclusions are then drawn from distorted information
– but issued in the name of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
You blatantly ignore civilian casualties on the Russian Side
, claiming that 95% of civilian casualties occur in territory controlled by Kiev. At the same time, you attribute nine out of ten crimes involving sexual violence to Russia,
without the slightest basis
.
👉
How can there be any talk of objectivity in these circumstances?
There is little point in analysing the reports of
the so-called UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine
. Every quarter, it presents the world with
increasingly absurd conclusions based on unreliable data.
But what can you expect from a body established under a bilateral agreement between Kiev and OHCHR back in 2014,
funded by generous contributions from Western donors
and receiving information exclusively from Kiev?!
Does anyone believe it is impartial?
❗️
Meanwhile,
attacks by Ukrainian militants
since 2022 alone have resulted in
more than 36,400 civilian casualties, including 9,141 deaths
– and we are ready to substantiate these figures.
Mr High Commissioner, do you not think there is now
an urgent need for an open discussion at the intergovernmental level of the methodology
used by the UN, and OHCHR in particular, to collect and verify data?
☝️
I hope such a step could at least partly restore States’ trust in you, High Commissioner, and in the Office you head.
#KievRegimeCrimes

#Victory81
🌟
#OTD
in 1943, Zaporozhye was liberated by the Red Army during the
Battle of the Dnieper
.
The city of
#Zaporozhye
, which by that time had become a
major industrial and logistics hub
, was occupied by the Nazi invaders in the first months of the Great Patriotic War.
◼️
During two years of
Nazi terror
and
occupation
, more than 40'000 civilians and POWs were killed in Zaporozhye by the enemy troops.
The Nazis sought to hold the city at any cost, as it had become a key stronghold in the lower reaches of the Dnieper. The Germans had effectively turned Zaporozhye into a major bridgehead within the system of fortifications along the '
Eastern Wall
' defence line.
⚔️
In the autumn of 1943, the front line was rapidly approaching the Dnieper. On October 4, the units of the Red Army’s Southwestern Front, commanded by would-be Marshal of the Soviet Union
Rodion Yakovlevich Malinovsky
,
launched an offensive in the Zaporozhye sector
.
Having breached the Germans’ outer defence on October 13, the Soviet forces approached the city.
Fierce combat raged for every street, every residential building.
By the end of the day on October 14, following a night-time assault, the Red Army had overcome enemy resistance and liberated Zaporozhye.
The Nazis were deprived of a strategically important bridgehead on the eastern bank of the Dnieper and lost the ability to launch a counterattack. Unable to stop the Red Army’s advance during its the Zaporozhye peration, the Nazi command ordered the Dnieper Hydroelectric Power Plant (DnieproGES) dam to be blown up.
📄
From the testimony given during an interrogation on October 11, 1947 by
Kurt Hans Steffen, a former driver with the 520th Engineer Regiment,
holding the rank of Obergefreiter:
There were five concealed, well-camouflaged explosive charge sites at the power station and four camouflaged charge sites on the dam itself...
We received the order to blow up DnieproGES from Major Senftenberg (commander of the 520th Engineer Regiment battalion — editorial note). The explosion was intended to destroy and demolish DnieproGES.
“Leave nothing but scorched earth in our path of retreat” — that is exactly what we did.
🎖
The success of the Zaporozhye Offensive Operation, carried out in just four days, opened the way for Red Army units and formations to advance towards
#
KrivoyRog
. It also enabled Soviet forces to outflank the Nazi troops in the Melitopol area. Its defeat paved the way for the liberation of
#
Melitopol
on October 23.
#Victory81
#WeRemember

🎙
Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova’s
answers to questions
from Izvestia regarding Montenegro’s introduction of a visa regime for Russian citizens
(October 14, 2026)
❓
Question: Previously, the Montenegrin authorities announced the introduction of
a visa regime for Russian citizens
effective November 1. Has the Montenegrin side provided any clarifications in this regard? How will this decision affect relations between Moscow and Podgorica? Are any retaliatory measures planned?
Maria Zakharova:
Yes, on September 28, the Montenegrin Foreign Ministry notified the Russian Side of
the termination
of
the Agreement between the Government of the Russian Federation and the Government of Montenegro on the terms of reciprocal travel for citizens
of September 24, 2008.
According to the clarifications received, in practice this means that, from November 1,
our citizens will only be able to enter Montenegro and stay in the country with a visa
. Accordingly,
Montenegrin citizens will also have to obtain visas to travel to Russia
.
❗️
Podgorica’s decision obviously damages Montenegro’s own interests.
The groundwork laid over many years in Russian-Montenegrin relations is being consistently dismantled to cater to European aspirations
, and due attention is not being paid to the economic consequences of such steps.
Undoubtedly, the introduction of a visa regime will
reduce the tourist flow from Russia
,
damage Montenegrin businesse
s and
worsen the investment climate
. At the same time, it is, of course, pointless for the Montenegrin authorities to count on any compensation from Brussels for the inevitable losses.
***
❓
Question: It has recently emerged that the EU has begun drawing up clear, phased plans for the accession of Albania, Moldova, Ukraine and Montenegro. At the same time, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia and Serbia also hold EU candidate status in the Balkans. How does Russia view the continuation of European integration of the Balkan countries, given the EU’s drift towards becoming a military bloc?
Maria Zakharova:
How to build relations with the EU is
a sovereign choice for the Balkan countries themselves,
which, incidentally, have been waiting in the queue to join the EU for decades (
Albania
since 2000,
North Macedonia
since 2004,
Montenegro
since 2008, and
Serbia
since 2009).
Over this period, the EU has, of course, changed greatly, and
by no means for the better
. This concerns
both its economic metrics
and
the way it acts on the international stage
.
Frenzied militarisation, a failed migration policy, and a wholly irrational renunciation of trade and energy cooperation with Russia –
all of this has had an extremely negative impact on the socioeconomic situation in Europe
.
The referendum in Iceland in August this year
, in which the island’s population voted against resuming EU membership negotiations,
clearly demonstrated that the EU has lost its appeal.
☝️
The EU’s drift towards becoming a military blo
c, coupled with the declaration of Russia as the principal existential threat for the long term (including “beyond the horizon” of the end of the conflict in and around Ukraine),
has also fundamentally altered the essence of the EU enlargement
. This process no longer in any way implies that new members can retain a neutral status.
